III—BATTLES FOUGHT IN PERTHSHIRE    SOME EARLY PERTHSHIRE BATTLES    WITH A NOTE ON  THE SIEGES OF PERTH    By SIR ALEXANDER MUIR MACKENZIE or De vine, Bart.    From the earliest times down to those almost within our own memories, this  county has been the scene of important battles.   Perthshire is divided by the chain of mountains which traverses the county  from south-west to north-east—the “ Dorsum Britanniz,” ‘‘The Mounth,”  “The Grampians,” call it what you will—into two main portions—the broad,  peaceful straths on the south, and the rugged fastnesses on the north.   Amid scenes of now woodland and pastoral beauty, battles have been fought

the regiment for upwards of  seventeen years.   General M‘Nab died unmarried on January the 7th, 1790, at his house in  St. James’s Square, Edinburgh,! and was interred at the burying-place of his  family near Killin.    1 Edinburgh Evening Courant, 11th January 1790. Can honour’s voice provoke the silent dust,  Or flattery soothe the dull, cold ear of death ?”  —Tuomas Gray.    I. GENERAL THE RIGHT HON. SIR DAVID BAIRD, BART.,  G.C.B., K.C.,! 1757-1829    ON a wooded knowe in the very centre of Strath Earn, just where it narrows  from its lowland to its mountainous aspect—commanding the woods of Strowan,  the windings of the Earn, the sunny slopes of Monzievaird and Ochtertyre—  there stands a monumental obelisk which challenges the question of every  stranger, and has contrived, though struck by lightning, to defy nearly a  century of storms.
